---

\frametitle{Review: Big Picture}

What is the point of building a model?

>- \textbf{Prediction} 

>- \textbf{Comparison}

---

\frametitle{Review: Big Picture}

>- \textbf{Regression is a mathematical tool for making predictions.}

>- Regression coefficients can always be interpreted as average comparisons of predictions.

>- Regression coefficients can sometimes be interpreted as effects.

---

\frametitle{Review: Big Picture}

\includegraphics[page=1,width = 1\textwidth]{figures/epistemology.pdf}

---

\frametitle{Review: Big Picture}

>- Generalization:
>   - \textbf{Constructs:} Do our measures generalize to concepts?
>   - \textbf{Target population:} Does our sample generalize to the population?
>   - \textbf{Forecasting:} Does our model of the present generalize to the future?
>   - \textbf{Causal inference:} Does our comparison generalize to a causal effect?

---

\frametitle{Review: Big Picture}

What do we need in order to interpret our comparison as a causal effect?

>- \textbf{Internal validity} (e.g., exchangeability)

>- \textbf{External validity} (e.g., transportability)

---

\frametitle{Review: Models}

What does it mean to "build" a model?

---

\frametitle{Review: Models}

>- \textbf{Estimand:} What is my goal? What is my target comparison I want to infer something about? Example: I want to know if income varies by education, conditional on age.

>- \textbf{Estimator:} How do I relate my population estimand to real sample data in a way that let's me identify its _most likely_ value given that sample data? 

>- \textbf{Estimation:} How do I optimize my estimator (i.e., calculate the most likely value of my estimand)? 

---

\frametitle{Review: Models}

1. \textbf{Estimand:} Choose a functional form for the model and highlight the target parameter ("estimand").

$$y_i=\beta_0+\boxed{\beta_1}{x_i}+\epsilon_i$$

2. \textbf{Estimator:} Choose an estimator that relates the model to real observed data (e.g., OLS) and is unbiased, consistent, and efficient.

$$\text{Sum of squared residuals}=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\widehat{\beta_0}-\widehat{\beta_1}x_i)^2$$

3. \textbf{Estimation:} Estimate parameters by optimizing the estimator; sometimes this can be done analytically, sometimes it requires brute computational force.

---

\frametitle{Review: Statistical Inference}

>- Our models consist of a set of \textbf{parameters:} the unknown numbers (random variables) that determine a statistical model.

>- We often want to do \textbf{statistical inference} on these parameters because they represent comparisons that map to our research questions. 

>- This involves \textbf{uncertainty}. 

---

\frametitle{Review: Statistical Inference}

>- Estimate the \textbf{standard error} based on the concept of the \textbf{sampling distribution.}
>   - The standard error depends on sample variability and sample size. 

>- How do we estimate the standard error?
>   - Analytic approach: formulas.
>   - Simulation approach: bootstrapping.

---

\frametitle{Review: Statistical Inference}

>- For inference, we use the \textbf{p-value:} the probability that the null model would produce a parameter estimate as extreme as your observed estimate if the null model is correct.

>- Our convention is that a p-value of less than 0.05 represents "statistical significance." 

---

\frametitle{Review: Causal Inference}

>- \textbf{Why might we want to add multiple predictors to our models?}
>   - We want to isolate a more specific comparison (e.g., age standardization).
>   - We want to estimate a causal effect, so we control for confounders.

---

\frametitle{Review: Causal Inference}

>- The fundamental problem of causal inference.
>   - We can only ever see one outcome at one time for any given unit, even though they have multiple _potential outcomes_. 

>- We can attempt to estimate \textbf{average treatment effects} by predicting potential outcomes. 

---

\frametitle{Review: Causal Inference}

>- \textbf{Causal inference is a prediction problem:} we must predict potential outcomes using average observed outcomes from exchangeable units.

>- The regression model is one way of generating the predictions needed to estimate the ATE.

---

\frametitle{Review: Causal Inference}

>- \textbf{Confounder:} any variable that affect both the likelihood of treatment and likelihood of outcome.

>- \textbf{Mediator:} any variable on the causal pathway between treatment and outcome.

>- \textbf{Moderator:} any variable that affects the relationship between treatment and outcome. 

---

\frametitle{Review: Panel Data}

>- \textbf{Panel data:} A data set where we observe the same units (e.g., individuals, firms, countries, schools) over more than one time period. 

>- New estimator: fixed effects. 

>- Fixed effects for the unit of analysis removes time-invariant confounding. 

>- Do I care about within- or between-unit variation for my research question?

---

\frametitle{Review: Assumptions}

Key assumptions:

* Validity
* Representativeness
* \textbf{Additivity and linearity}
* Independence of errors
* Equal variance of errors
* Normality of errors

---

\frametitle{Review: Assumptions}

>- Linear transformations
>   - Shifting (i.e., add/subtract a constant)
>   - Rescaling (i.e., multiply/divide by a constant)

---

\frametitle{Review: Assumptions}

>- Non-linear transformations
>   - Logs
>   - Polynomials
>   - Splines

---

\frametitle{Review: Assumptions}

When do we think about \textbf{transforming} continuous variables or including \textbf{interactions}?

>- \textbf{Predictive model}
>   - Try everything and use cross-validation to see if it improves out-of-sample fit.

>- \textbf{Causal model}
>   - Examining heterogeneous treatment effects (transform/interact the treatment variable).
>   - Relaxing assumptions about confounding pathways (transform/interact the confounder variables).

---

\frametitle{Applied Quantitative Research}

>- Steps for an applied quantitative research project

---

\frametitle{Applied Quantitative Research}

>- \textbf{(1)} Read the literature. What do we know? What do we not know? Draw a conceptual model to guide your research question.

>- \textbf{(2)} Familiarize yourself with the data. Can we use existing data? Do we need new data?

>- \textbf{(3)} Refine conceptual model into a DAG (this may include drawing the "causal field") that is specific about measurement of _constructs_ and definition of _target population_. 

>- \textbf{(4)} Specify the _estimand_ that answers your research question. In other words, choose a functional form for the model and highlight your target parameter (e.g., $\beta_1$).

---

\frametitle{Applied Quantitative Research}

>- \textbf{(5)} Load data into R. Make descriptive summary statistics and plots. Revisit Steps 1-4 as needed.

>- \textbf{(6)} Choose estimator (e.g., OLS) and fit model. 

>- \textbf{(7)} Test for non-linearity and non-additivity in the relationship between treatment and outcome.

\frametitle{Why should we understand quantitative methods (and coding)?}

>- \textbf{There is some inherent value.} Quantitative methods can provide empirical, falsifiable facts about the social world (but not what those facts mean!); for example, how did different groups vote in 2024, and was this different from how those groups voted in 2020?

>- \textbf{They will be used in your field.} You will have to understand and critique quantitative studies, even if they are outside the methodology you use in your own research.

>- \textbf{Non-academic careers.}

>- \textbf{Organizing/advocacy.}

---

\frametitle{Quantitative methods}

>- \textbf{Empiricism:} social theories imply empirical claims that are falsifiable.

>- Data doesn't speak for itself; it must be carefully interpreted, summarize, and analyzed.

---

\frametitle{Review}

Spirling & Stewart (2025): Inference to best explanation (IBE). 

"Research contributions therefore fall into three overlapping types:  the generation of explanations, the production of facts, and the updating of explanations in  light of those facts."

---

\frametitle{Review}

"We emphasize three ideas:

>- First, IBE often involves the  bringing together of multiple pieces of evidence: e.g. many different regressions in various  places, in addition to a qualitative case study on a potential mechanism.

>- Second, explanation  is obviously vital to the practice of IBE, and should be taken as seriously as inference is.

>- Third, that exploratory analysis, because it encourages the development of explanations, is  similarly crucial and currently undervalued."

>   - Advanced \textbf{instrument-based} methods (e.g., IVs, diff-in-diff).

>- Survey design

>- Advanced predictive models (i.e., "machine learning")

\frametitle{Introduction to the course}

>- It’s easy to feel totally overwhelmed and totally behind. Quantitative methods can seem like a huge list of rules that you just don't "get" - and have no hope of ever understanding. \textbf{This is not true.}

>- Norms, computation standards, etc. 

>- Generating knowledge is hard no matter what methods we use to do it.
